## Saddatthabhedacintāpāḷi
## Saddabhedacintā
1. Having paid homage to the Buddha—who is supreme among teachers who explain the distinctions of sounds and meanings, and who habitually teaches the noble Nibbāna—I shall compose the treatise *Saddatthabhedacintā*, which is the means for knowing the distinctions of sounds and meanings.

2. Sound is of two kinds: mind-born (*cittaja*) sound, such as the letter 'A' and others, and physical (*utuja*) sound, such as the sound of the stomach and others. Among these two, only mind-born sound is taken in this treatise because it serves the purpose of conveying meaning.

3. That mind-born sound is also known to be produced by the striking of the earth elements against each other, which occurs due to vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), a power of the mind-born earth element at the vocal bases such as the throat, where it becomes manifest.

4. Other teachers know that it is produced in the head because the *pāṇa* wind, rising upwards due to the effort of wanting to recite from the region of the navel, strikes the vocal bases such as the chest and throat.

5. Because of its benefit to the Dispensation (*Sāsana*), the Māgadha language is taken in this treatise. That Māgadha language is the cause for the hearing of the Dhamma and for the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*).
2: 6. The sound of each individual letter in a word that has not yet been fully recited is called ultimate sound (paramattha-sadda). A word that has been fully recited is called conceptual sound (paññatti-sadda). In this way, Māgadha sound is of two kinds. 7. Although there are more than one sound in terms of being heard by the ear, those sounds are called 'one word' in the world. This is because they are designated in the world as 'one word' due to their ability to signify a single meaning. 8. A word consisting of a single letter, as well as a word consisting of more than one letter, is designated as one if it signifies a single meaning. A vowel, or a consonant together with that vowel, is designated as a single letter. 9. Even though there are many words, they are called only 'one word' because they are delimited by a particle (nipāta) and because those words possess a single meaning. 10. The word 'Ā' occurs in the sense of 'excessive'; the word 'I' occurs in the sense of 'going.' In these examples, 'Ā' and 'I' are words consisting of a single letter. The words 'itthī' and 'puriso' are words consisting of many letters. Many words such as 'yaṃ kiñci' and 'apeti' also attain the state of being a single word.
3: 11. A word makes the meaning known when it becomes an object of auditory consciousness and when it has been established by convention (that 'this word signifies this meaning'). If these two causes—being an object of auditory consciousness and being established by convention—are absent, it cannot make the meaning known. 12. A collection of various words that depends on the common usage of people, that exists as modifiers (visesana) and the modified (visesya), and that clearly expresses a complete meaning according to the speaker's intention, is called a sentence (vākya). 13. In a word that has not yet been fully recited, each individual sound is called a letter (akkhara). When the recitation is finished, it is called a word (pada). A collection of those words is called a sentence (vākya). That sentence has the characteristic of mutual dependence. 14. In a sentence, there are five components as appropriate: the proposition (paṭiññā), the illustration (upamā), the reason (hetu), the example (udāharaṇa), and the conclusion (nigama). 15. Just as fire is known in a kitchen through heat and smoke, so too (fire is known through heat and smoke). If it is asked, 'Where is the fire?', because the fire, which is the thing to be illustrated (upameyya), is not manifest, it is pointed out as 'on the mountain top'.

In the doctrine of those teachers, would it not be that there could never be a corruption of sound (apasadda)? 19. Even if a corrupted sound is spoken due to lack of mindfulness or due to laziness, the state of the correct sound is known when searching for and considering the meaning. 5: 21. Just as a marble that was swallowed and hidden is brought out and shown again, so too this artificial sound is called permanent sound (nicca-sadda). Just as a divine image is called a 'deva,' so too this impermanent artificial sound is called the real permanent sound. 22. Some grammarians, who are proponents of both permanence and impermanence, say that sound is impermanent and momentary because it is something made, like a pot and the like. 23. In the view of teachers of permanence like Piṃsala, because sounds are permanent, names of compounds (samāsa) and names like Ga, Pa, Jha, La, etc., are known only as conventional names (rūḷhī-nāma). However, in the view of the teachers of impermanence, they are also known as derivative names (anvattha-nāma) according to the meaning. 24. A thing that has no cause is called permanent; a thing that follows causes is called impermanent. This sound cannot be called permanent because it arises in vocal bases such as the throat. 25. Nevertheless, it cannot be called impermanent either, because it occurs in the lineage of speech of the ancients and because it exists by way of the conventions (saṅketa) of the ancients. Therefore, the treatise on grammar is composed for the purpose of establishing conventions. 26. The meanings of a word should be known as fivefold, as appropriate: its own meaning (sakattha), substance (dabba), gender (liṅga), number (saṅkhyā), and the factors of action (kāraka) such as the object (kamma).

The five meanings of a word should be known as appropriate: sakattha, substance (dabba), gender (liṅga), number (saṅkhyā), and the factors of action (kāraka) such as the object. 27. It is called 'attha' (meaning) because it is known. Or, it is called 'attha' because it is specified by this modifier (visesana). The modifier that belongs to itself (the modified/visesya) is called 'saka'. Since that 'saka' is itself the meaning, it is called 'sakattha'. That sakattha is indeed the modifier (visesana). 28. (Sakattha) has seven distinctions: audition (suti), genus (jāti), quality (guṇa), substance (dabba), relation (sambandha), action (kriyā), and the relation of action and its factors (kriyā-kāraka-sambandha). 29. Alternatively, sakattha should be known as eightfold, including similarity (sadisa) and the like. The wise know that sakattha as the meaning of the modifier (visesana) that distinguishes the modified (visesya). 30. Whatever object (matter) is understood by the uttered sound, that object is known by the name 'attha' (meaning) of that sound.

31. Just as a lamp reveals (itself as a lamp), so too grammar (sadda) reveals the auditory perception (suti) called sarūpa, which is the cause of the collective word and always follows the word.

32. The commonality (sāmañña) that produces non-distinct knowledge and words regarding diverse substances such as a brindled cow is called genus (jāti). That genus follows substances just as a string follows the flowers in a garland.

33. That common genus is both permanent and pervasive. In entities such as 'existence' (satta) and 'cow-ness' (gava), ancient teachers call them 'great generality' (mahāsāmañña) and 'specific generality' (visesasāmañña) respectively.

34. Quality (guṇa) is known as an entity that depends on a substance, is distinct from that substance, is the cause of knowing the distinction of that substance, is subject to change, and possesses no quality of its own.

35. Relation (sambandha) is distinct from the six kārakas; it is preceded by action (kriyā) and kāraka (such as giving and taking); it produces knowledge of the two related entities (sambandhī) and depends on those two related entities.

36. Relation (sambandha) cannot be seen in its concrete form at any time like the related substances (sambandhī). Therefore, the wise who are proficient know that relation through inference (anumāna).

36. Relation (sambandha) is not something that can be seen in its concrete form like the related entities (sambandhī). Therefore, wise and discerning scholars can only know that relation through inference (anumāna).

37. In the occurrence of "The King gives, the man takes," relation arises based on the actions of giving and taking, characterized by mutual dependence.

38. The genitive case (chaṭṭhī) occurs in the sense of the remaining related substance (sambandhī) apart from the kāraka that completes the action. That genitive case also illuminates the relation (sambandha). However, if the relation is already expressed by a compound (samāsa) or a derivative (taddhita), that genitive case is elided.

39. Alternatively, to further clarify the relation expressed by two related substances, the genitive case is applied to the qualifier (visesana) of the qualified (visesya). This is because the genitive case possesses the linguistic power (sadda-satti) to express the meaning of relation only when it follows a qualifier.

40. The meaning of the root (dhātu) is itself called action (kriyā). If one asks what that action is, it is effort (īhā). If one asks what that effort is, it is instigation (jeṭṭhakā). If one asks what that instigation is, it is the activity (byāpāra) occurring in the body. That bodily activity itself is known as action.

41. Although that action (kriyā) cannot be seen concretely like a substance as "this very thing," it is known by inferring from states such as the lifting of a foot or the softness of cooked rice.

42. Although that action is known by inference, it is manifest along with the power of the kārakas. Being established by worldly convention, it is known depending on substance.

43. The scholar who knows action says that the meaning which is not a substance, which resides in the agent (kattu) and the object (kamma), and which is accomplished by the group of kārakas, is to be known as "action" (kriyā). Other wise men also know it thus.

44. Whatever is qualified is a substance along with its qualifier (visesana). The qualified (visesya) is the meaning of the support, and the qualified exists together with the qualifier.

45. Qualifiers occur and reside in this qualified; therefore, it is called substance (dabba). That substance is fourfold. It is divided by genus (jāti), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and substance (dabba).

46. A certain mode such as masculinity (pumatta), which is conceived by the intellect and is the meaning of conventional usage like the faculty of masculinity (purisindriya), is called the meaning of gender (liṅga).

47. An object such as a son is said to be similar to an object such as a father. Even though they are similar, the son cannot be the father himself. Because of the similarity between the distinct son and father, the state of simile and metaphor (upamā-upameyya) arises between them.

48. According to the view of the Atthasālinī Commentary, gender (liṅga) is known as the conceived shape of large hands and feet, etc., which occurs along with the masculine faculty in the continuity of a man.

49. Other teachers say that the meaning of gender is the three-fold movement such as walking, characterized by purity, etc. Some other teachers, however, say that gender refers to beards, hair, and so forth.

50. In treatises such as the Candra, the meaning of gender is desired as merely the meaning of the completed gender-word. In treatises such as the Kalāpa, however, the wise who know the meaning desire the meaning of the uncompleted gender-word as the meaning of gender.

51. In the Dispensation (Pali literature), the singular (ekavacana) and the plural (bahuvacana) are called number (saṅkhyā). In Sanskrit, however, the wise include the dual (dvivacana) when speaking of number.

52. Including the bhāva-kāraka as the seventh, the kārakas starting with the object are called kammādi-kāraka. That kāraka is to be known through the agent-instrument (kattu-sādhana) or the state-instrument (bhāva-sādhana).

53. Among the five types of meanings—substance, quality, action, genus, and name—that meaning which accomplishes the action residing in the agent or the action residing in the object is called kāraka.

54. Just as something non-existent in the world is conventionally treated as existent, by this logic, bhāva (action), though having no physical form, is to be regarded as a kāraka through the method of kattu-sādhana.

55. Alternatively, the act of doing (karaṇa) or action is called kāra (making), and that kāra itself is kāraka. Because of these two sādhanas, kāraka is of two types: satti-kāraka (potentiality) and kriyā-kāraka (action).

56. Is it not true that potentiality (satti) is not manifest apart from substance and other objects? In this context, why do you desire the non-visible potentiality as kāraka while discarding the directly visible substance?

57. That capability of a substance which accomplishes an action is called potentiality (satti). Due to that potentiality, a substance becomes an agent (kattu), or an instrument (karaṇa), etc.

58. Just as a single cloth is differentiated into various types due to its association with color-qualities such as blue or yellow, so too a substance, though one, is differentiated into various types due to its association with potentialities such as the agent (kattu).

61. Because it accomplishes the action, only the power (satti) is the actual (mukha) kāraka. The substance (dabba) is called kāraka by way of metonymy (ṭhānyūpacāra) because it is the locus of that power.

62. In the expression "The word says the meaning," the word should be taken as a substance. The word that expresses the meaning is also called kāraka by way of causal metonymy (kāraṇūpacāra) because of the cause which is the meaning.

63. An object that is the cause of an action and certainly results in the action is called kāraka. An object that is merely a cause of an action but does not result in the action is called akāraka.

64. Meanings such as the possessive (sāmī), vocative (ālapana), and partitive (niddhāraṇabhāgī) should be understood as akāraka because they lack connection with the action at that moment.

65. Meanings such as the characteristic of state (bhāvalakkhaṇa) and cause (hetu) are not called kāraka, even if they are connected to or are the cause of that action, because they do not result in the action.

Kāraka is of six types due to the differences in the moments of power and the distinctions of agent (kattu), instrument (karaṇa), object (kamma), recipient (sampadāna), limit (avadhi), and locus (okāsa). 67. The kāraka that performs the action—whether located in itself or in the object—which is preceded by other kārakas such as the instrument and is invariably associated with all actions, is called the agent (kattu). 68. The agent pervades all actions. The remaining five kārakas, such as the object, pervade only specific actions. Thus, kāraka is known to be of two kinds. 69. This agent is of three types: the pure agent (suddha-kattu), the causal agent (hetu-kattu), and the object-agent (kamma-kattu). (For example:) Datta performs [the action] himself; he causes [another] to perform; the drinking water drinks itself. 70. The kāraka that provides the greatest assistance to the agent in accomplishing the action is called the instrument (karaṇa). That instrument is said to have superior power over all other kārakas besides the agent.

71. The instrument kāraka (karaṇa) is of two types: the external (bāhira/bāhya) instrument and the internal (ajjhatta/abbhantara) instrument. (For example:) One reaps rice with a sickle; one sees the moon with the eye.

72. The kāraka that is reached (connected) by the action is called the object (kamma). In the sense of the objective derivative (kammasādhana), the power of being reached by the action is called kamma. Furthermore, the action itself is called kamma due to the sense of the abstract derivative (bhāvasādhana).

73. The object (kamma) is known to be of three types: the produced object (nipphatti-kamma), the transformed object (vikati-kamma), and the reached object (patti-kamma). (For example:) One makes a mat; one burns wood; one worships the sun.

74. The kāraka to whom something is well-given is called the recipient (sampadāna). That recipient has the characteristic of receiving either the substance or the action.

75. A substance given with the desire to honor or to favor is considered "well-given." Only when the recipient becomes the owner of the given substance is that kāraka called sampadāna.

76. In examples such as "Gives clothes to the washerman" or "Gives a fine to the king," the status of sampadāna cannot be established because there is no intention of honoring and so forth.

77. Sampadāna is of three types: the consented recipient (anumati-sampadāna), the non-rejected recipient (anirākattu-sampadāna), and the propitiated recipient (ārādhaka-sampadāna). "Gives to a monk," "Waters a tree," and "Gives to a beggar" are the respective examples.

78. Sampadāna is of two types: that preceded by physical attainment (kāyasampatti-pubba) and that preceded by mental attainment (cittasampatti-pubba). "Gives robes to a monk" and "Gives offerings to the god Nārāyaṇa" are their respective examples.

79. Although the separation of two objects is equal, the object that remains fixed in its previous state without moving is called the ablative (apādāna). This apādāna has the characteristic of a limit (avadhi).

80. Apādāna is of two types: that preceded by mental reach (buddhisampatti-pubba) and that preceded by physical reach (kāyasampatti-pubba). Furthermore, it is of two types according to being moving (cala) and non-moving (acala). Examples include "[Danger] from a thief" and "[Ascetics depart] from the village."

81. Apādāna is known to be of three types: (1) niddiṭṭhavisaya-apādāna, where the action is explicitly indicated; (2) upāttavisaya-apādāna, where the action is implied; and (3) anumeyyavisaya-apādāna, where the action is inferred.

82. Sages depart from the village. One cooks rice (taking it) from the granary. These [Mathurans] are more beautiful than the Pāṭaliputrans.

83. The agent and the object, which are the supports of the action, reside in a certain kāraka. That locus itself is called okāsa by way of indirect metonymy (paramparūpacāra).

84. Since the agent and the object have already acquired specific names, they should not be called okāsa. For it is said that a specific name overrides a general name.

85. Support (ādhāra) is of four types: (1) pervasive (vyāpika, e.g., sesame), (2) contactual (opasilesika, e.g., a pot), (3) sphere-based (vesayika, e.g., the sky), and (4) proximal (sāmīpika, e.g., the Ganges river).

86. Support is also of two types: primary (padāna) and conceptual (parikappa); or primary (mukha) and metaphorical (upacāra). Examples are like sesame and the Ganges river.
18: 86. Support (ādhāra) is of two types: primary support and conceptual support. Furthermore, it is of two types: primary (mukha) and metaphorical (upacāra). Examples are the presence of oil in sesame (tila) and the location of a village on the Ganges (gaṅgā). 87. In this same way, all words are divided into primary (mukha) and non-primary (amukha). The sentences "One bathes in the Ganges" and "Crops grow on the Ganges" are examples of primary and non-primary respectively. 88. Transgressing the true meaning to regard a non-true meaning, or regarding a part of the true meaning, is called metaphor (upacāra). 89. Examples such as "The lion sings" and "This youth is a lion" are of two types. They occur due to undifferentiated metaphor (abhedavivāchā) and the identity connection (soyaṃ-sambandha) where "that person is this person." 90. The meaning associated with a case ending such as 'aṃ' which depends on another verbal word is called kāraka. The object that is the meaning of the suffix together with the root is called sādhana. 91. Alternatively, a kāraka in a sentence becomes a sādhana when it is completed as a derivative (kit) word. That same sādhana becomes the six types of kāraka again when connected with case endings. This is their distinction. 92. One should understand the analysis: "He who cooks rice, therefore he is a pācaka (cook)," and examples such as "The pācaka eats."

91. In another way, whatever kāraka exists in a sentence, that same kāraka becomes a sādhana when it is manifest (as a kit derivative). Within this kit term, that sādhana can again become the six kārakas. This occurrence is the distinction between kāraka and sādhana.

92. Whoever cooks rice, because of that ability to cook, that person is called a 'pācaka' (cook). That same cook eats the rice. Such examples should be understood.

93. Meaning (attha) is fivefold by way of substance (dabba), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), name (nāma), and genus (jāti). Other wise men say that based on the meaning, the word (sadda) is also divided into five.

94. A horned ox (vīsāṇī), a white ox (dhavalo), a walking ox (gantā), an ox named Citta (citto), and an ox (go)—thus do the wise refer to the meanings such as substance and the words such as dabba-sadda respectively.

95. In the Pāḷi text explaining Niruttipaṭisambhidā, each individual letter is called 'nāmapaññatti' because of its distinct arising.

96. Some teachers say that a collection called a sequence of letters is 'nāma' because it clearly manifests the meaning. If that were so, all words such as dabba-sadda would also become nāma.

97. All words such as dabba-sadda would become nāma. In reality, a name is merely a type of human convention (saṅketa) that clearly indicates the object to be named (saññī-dabba).

Cognition (buddhi) arises from the expression of its own meaning (sak-attha); it is not known through a qualifier (visesana). Generally, it is understood by way of the qualified (visessya). 99. Because of being associated with the sound, because of being known by the nature of that sound, and because of being general (sāmañña), first the auditory perception (suti) and the genus (jāti) are perceived. 100. That substance (dabba) follows the specific (visesa) and also follows the general (sāmañña). Because they are the basis for gender (liṅga) and number (saṅkhyā), these are mentioned later.

101. Since gender depends only on substance, gender is mentioned after that substance. Number also depends on that substance, but because it has the function of excluding other numbers, it is mentioned after gender.

102. A word can effect a restriction in the meaning known through methods such as upalakkhaṇā, either by the power of the word 'eva' or by the exclusion of other meanings (aññatthāpohana).

103. Although kāraka (sādhana) depends on substance, because it regards the action (bhāva), it is mentioned after number. Because it depends on another, two groups of four are made: the kammādi-catutthaka and the saṅkhyā-catutthaka.

104. The three meanings such as gender are included in substance because they have substance as their locus. Substance is also included in the own-meaning (sak-attha) because it qualifies other substances.

105. Because those meanings such as suti are the qualified, only the six own-meanings (sak-attha) are included (in substance). Genus (jāti) and so on, although they are own-meanings, are called 'dabbata' because they exist in substance.

106. One should observe the preceding and succeeding order without contradicting the author's intention. What is the use of searching for a fixed sequence? It is only due to reasons such as proximity (paccāsatti).

## Saddatthabhedacintā

107. When knowing the meaning through an undivided word, the meaning is also perceived as undivided. This is because it is not differentiated by the intellect. For example, the word 'citra' in words like 'citrago' (variegated cow) and 'citra-asso' (variegated horse).

108. Just as in words like 'citrago', the variegation such as whiteness is differentiated by the intellect, similarly, if the stem (pakati) and suffix (paccaya) are differentiated, only the distinct meanings are perceived.

109. The stem (pakati) consists only of gender (liṅga) and root (dhātu), while inflections (vibhatti) and suffixes are called 'paccaya'. Some teachers say that words ending in nominal inflections like 'si' or verbal inflections like 'ti' are also stems (pakati).

110. When suffixes such as taddhita, ākhyāta, and kita, or compounds (samāsa), or nominal inflections like 'si', or roots and genders are differentiated, the meaning also becomes distinct.
