111. A wise person who sees the distinctions of word-meanings should understand the meaning of a word as a group of two, a group of three, a group of four, or even a group of five.

112. In examples such as 'paṭvī' (a clever woman), because this letter (ī) is an expresser (vācaka) of the feminine gender, the meaning of the word is known as a group of two, consisting of the word alone without connection to suffixes, inflections, or verbs.

113. In the same examples like 'paṭvī', because this letter is an indicator (jotaka) of the feminine gender, the meaning of the word is known as a group of three by the word alone.

114. The own-meaning (sak-attha), the substance (dabba) known by that own-meaning, and the gender (liṅga) residing in that substance—this threefold division always resides in a word.

115. The group of four (catukk-attha) is of two kinds. In examples such as 'māsajāta' (born a month ago), the group of meanings where number is the fourth is known. Some teachers say that in the example 'māsika', that same saṅkhyā-catutthaka is known.

116. In answering the question, "What is the extent of the boy's age?", it is said, "He has been born for one month." In another way (if said alone), the name "one month" would mean only thirty days.
24: 116. When asked, "What is the extent of the boy's age?", one answers, "It is one month for this born boy." Otherwise (if said in isolation), the name "one month" would merely be thirty days. 117. Depending on the two words (māsa and jāta), the measure is specifically known as number (saṅkhyā). The number can be known from the question itself. In examples like "a boy born two months ago," a double number is known through the digu compound. 118. In the phrase "a month has passed for this born boy," some say the sixth inflection (chaṭṭhī-vibhatti) is applied in the sense of disregard (anādara). Other wise men say, "His month is complete." 119. In examples like "pierced by an arrow," the group of four meanings (catukka) such as kamma-kāraka is known. The word "arrow" (salla) is mentioned either because it is expected (by the word 'pierced') or because of natural association. 120. In the Liṅgatthavivaraṇa, the fivefold meaning of gender is shown in examples like 'suppikaṃ'. In the Pañcakattha, five meanings are shown in examples like 'soppaṃ'.
25:
121. Goods purchased by a measure such as a winnowing basket are called 'suppika'. In this example (suppikaṃ), the fivefold meaning (pañcaka) is obtained because the suffix (-ṇika) denotes both the qualifier (the basket) and the qualified (the goods purchased).

122. Even though the word for 'measure' (pamāṇa) is not directly present, the meaning of measure is obtained either through the elision of the subsequent word, or because it is inherent in the taddhita meaning, or because the meaning can be understood through the power of the base and the suffix.

123. 'Suppana', 'suppina', and 'soppa' are abstract meanings (bhāva) signifying 'sleeping'. Since this abstract meaning is of a general (sāmañña) nature, it can be both masculine and neuter, and it exists only in the singular.

124. In nouns such as 'purisa', when inflections like 'aṃ' manifest the meaning in relation to verbs like 'passati', the fivefold meaning (pañcaka) is always obtained because it is the meaning of the original stem (pakati-liṅga).

125. In verbal forms (ākhyāta) starting with the root, based on the expressive power (vācakatta) of the inflections and suffixes, meanings such as the twofold (dvika) and others should be understood due to the relationship of qualifier and qualified, etc.
26:
126. Some teachers say that in verbal forms like "pacati", there is only a single meaning according to the root. However, when there is the manifestation (jotana) by inflections and suffixes like 'ti', the wise person who knows the combination of word and meaning should understand meanings such as the threefold (tika).

127. In expletives (padapūraṇa) such as 'suttanta' and in euphonic combinations (sandhi) such as 'abhiratimiccheyya', a single meaning (euphony of speech) should be understood. Other wise men say that in examples like 'doṇika', a sixfold collection of meanings (chakka) should be understood through the distinctions of number and measure.

128. Just as a white object or similar utility in a dark room, though clearly existing, can only become manifest when there is light from a lamp or similar source; likewise, although meanings such as 'kamma' (object) clearly exist in the base (pakati) like 'purisa', they can only become manifest when there is an inflection (vibhatti).

129. Therefore, in the meaning of the base which is fivefold (pañcaka), and in the meaning of the base which is the fourfold number (saṅkhyā-catukka), the inflections are also the manifestors (jotika) of unmanifest meanings such as number and karma.

130. It is said that in the twofold (duka), threefold (tika), and the fourfold karma-related (kammādi-catukka) meanings of the base, the inflections are the expressors (vācika) of meanings such as number and karma.

131-132. A word first expresses its own meaning (sakattha), which is genus (jāti), quality (guṇa), and action (kriyā); after that, it expresses the substance (dabba) which is the locus of that own meaning; after that, it expresses gender (liṅga) such as feminine; after that, it expresses number (saṅkhyā) such as singular; after that, it expresses the six grammatical roles (kāraka) such as the object (kamma), with the possessive (sāmī) as the seventh. Therefore, other wise men say that the meaning of the base (liṅgattha) is only a fivefold collection (pañcaka).
27: 131. A word first expresses its own meaning (sakattha), which is genus (jāti), quality (guṇa), and action (kriyā); after that, it expresses the substance (dabba) which is the locus of that meaning; after that, it expresses gender (liṅga) such as feminine. 132. After that, it expresses number (saṅkhyā) such as singular, and the grammatical roles (kāraka) such as the object (kamma), including the possessive (sāmī). Therefore, other scholars know that the meaning of the base (liṅgattha) is a fivefold collection. 133. Both inflections (vibhatti) and feminine suffixes (itthi-paccaya) manifest the meaning of the base, number, grammatical roles like the object (kamma), and relation (sambandha) as appropriate. 134. These inflections and suffixes can manifest meanings because they occur in specific meanings and because the meanings become clear through those inflections and suffixes. Examples are: go (cow), sukko (white), pācako (cook), daṇḍī (one with a staff), gavaṃ (the cow [acc.]), goṇassa (of the cow), daṇḍinī (woman with a staff). 135. Even if there is only one meaning, it should be regarded as plural (bahuvacana) due to the metaphorical attribution of many meanings to one, or because it falls within the sequence of a plural teaching (desanā). 136. In Sanskrit grammar, the rule 'attani garūsu ca' (for oneself and for teachers) has been cited [for plural usage]. 'Mayaṃ gacchāma' (We go) and 'Tumhe ca gacchatha' (You [honorific] go) are examples in order.
28: 136. In Sanskrit grammar, the rule 'attani garūsu ca' has been cited. 'We go' (mayaṃ gacchāma) and 'You also go' (tumhe ca gacchatha) are examples in order. 137. The teacher of Dabbapadatthika named Vyāḍi says that because the form of the substance (dabba) is very clear, the uttered word primarily (mukhya) expresses the substance. 138. The teacher of Jātipadatthika named Vājabyāyana says that because the genus (jāti) is eternal, the uttered word primarily (padhāna) expresses the genus. 139. The Dabbapadatthika teacher says the meaning of a word is only the substance. The Jātipadatthika teacher says the meaning of a word is only the genus. Other wise men know this. 140. In truth, because the uttered word follows the sound, it always expresses its own form, which is the sound, and then primarily expresses either the substance or the genus.
29:
141. In the view of the Dabbapadatthika teacher, because it follows the substance which is its locus, the genus is also expressed secondarily (apadhāna). In the view of the Jātipadatthika teacher, because it is the locus of the genus, the substance is also expressed secondarily.

142. Substance (dabba), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), name (nāma), and relation (sambandha) are also expressed as appropriate. It should be understood that these, such as substance, are included in this way because they depend on the substance which is the locus of the genus (or are properties related to the substance).

143. Examples such as a cow (go), one with a staff (daṇḍī), a cook (pācako), a white thing (sukko), and a person named Diṭṭha (diṭṭha) are illustrations. A word like 'daṇḍī' (one with a staff) also expresses the genus of the object that is not separate from the staff.

144. That meaning such as sound (suti) which is called 'sakattha' (own meaning) is expressed secondarily by the word because it is the cause (nimitta) for the word's existence. That qualified meaning (visesya) which is called 'dabba' (substance) is expressed primarily by the word because it is the true meaning of the word.

145. The genus by which the qualified substance is called 'substance' is the 'sakattha'. Or (according to the Jātipadatthika view), the sound by which the genus is qualified is called 'substance', and that sound is the 'sakattha'. This is the case in words like 'cow' (go).

146. In examples such as 'the cow named Diṭṭha' and 'the name Diṭṭha of the cow', respectively: the substance of the cow is known through the name Diṭṭha, and the substance of the name Diṭṭha is known through the genus of the name Diṭṭha.
30:
146. In name-words such as "Diṭṭho go" (the ox named Diṭṭha) and "Gossa diṭṭhoti nāmaṃ" (the name of the ox is Diṭṭha), one should understand, respectively, the substance of the ox by the name 'Diṭṭha', and the substance of the name by the name-universal (nāma-jāti) 'Diṭṭha'.

147. Other teachers say that the name-universal is understood through sound (suti), and the name-substance included within the substance is understood through that name-universal; or otherwise, the substance is understood through the name.

148. In examples such as the white quality of an ox, only the quality-substance (guṇa-dabba) is understood through the quality-universal (guṇa-jāti). However, in examples such as "sukko go" (the white ox), the substance is understood only through the quality of whiteness.

149. Some teachers say, regarding the example "sukko gossa guṇo" (the white quality of the ox), that the quality-universal is understood through sound, or alternatively, the quality-substance is understood through the quality-universal, or the substance is understood through the quality.

150. In the context of compounds (samāsa) such as "chinnahattha" (one whose hand is cut) and in the context of derivatives (taddhita) such as "daṇḍī" (one who possesses a staff), substance is understood through substance; otherwise, substance is understood through the relation (sambandha) because that relation depends on the two related substances and connects them.
31:
151. Other wise ones say that (1) the universal (jāti) of that lineage (such as the one with a cut hand or the staff-bearer) is understood by the inherent nature of the sound; (2) the substance is understood by that universal; or (3) by the substance that is a component; or (4) by the connection of the relation (sambandha).

152. In primary derivatives (kita) of state (bhāva) such as "pāka" (cooking), and in verbal (ākhyāta) states such as "ṭhīyate" (standing), only the specific action-substance is understood through the general action-universal (kriyā-sāmañña-jāti). In verbs, since the action is primary, the same applies to words like "paccate" (it is cooked) and "pacati" (he cooks).

153. Other teachers say that in examples such as "paccate," "pacate," and "pācaka," the substance is understood either through the action or through the relation between the action and the agent (kāraka).

154. Some teachers say that the action-universal is understood through sound, the specific action through the action-universal, and furthermore, the substance is understood either through the relation between the action and the agent, or through the action itself.

155. In the sentence "Enter the staffs," the substance is understood either through substance or through the connection of relation. Examples such as "This youth is a lion" and "The man from the outer village is an ox" are likewise illustrative evidence.
32:
156. This metaphorical attribution (upacāra) to another substance occurs either because of association (sahacaraṇa), such as being with a staff, or because of having a nature similar to that lion or ox, such as bravery. Such metaphorical attribution exists only in name and not in the actual sense of the object.

157. Some teachers say that similarity (sadisa-bhāva) or relation (sambandha) is understood through sound. Alternatively, they say that substance is understood through substance, relation, similarity, and sound.

158. In expletives (padapūraṇa) and euphonic combinations (sandhi), the smoothness of the words is understood through sound. Since that smoothness is well-known in the world, the wise include it within the meaning of the substance.

159. According to the principle that "no sound is without meaning," the meaning of the original word is understood through the sound of the expletive. This is because the expletive word occurs only in the sense of the original word.

160. For this reason, cognition (buddhi) and sound (sadda) arise; therefore, that cause is called "bhāva" (state/cause). That 'bhāva' consists of substance (dabba), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), name (nāma), and universal (jāti), which are the causes for the occurrence of sound.
33:
161. The relation (sambandha) is included within the related substance (sambandhī) because it depends on that substance. The sound (suti) of a word is included within the universal (jāti) because it is the universal of the sound. Similarity (sādisya) is included within the similar substance (sadisa) because it depends on that similar substance.

162. Words with analytical meaning (vigraha) and words with non-analytical lexical meaning denote the etymological cause (byuppatti-nimitta) and the cause of linguistic usage (sadda-pavatti-nimitta) secondarily. Suffixes such as -ṇya are applied after these words to denote the sense of 'state' (bhāva). Furthermore, these suffixes are applied in the sense of 'good' (sādhu) and in their own sense (sakattha).

163. Cognition (buddhi) follows the cause of linguistic usage (sadda-pavatti-nimitta) and occurs in meanings such as substance. Likewise, the word arises because of the cause of linguistic usage.

164. Other wise ones know that the meaning of the cause of linguistic usage is the primary meaning of the word. In reality, however, the meaning of the cause of linguistic usage is the secondary meaning, and only the object qualified by that cause (visesya) is the primary meaning of the word.

165. The 'cow-ness' (gotta) of the cow-substance is simply the cow-universal (go-jāti). Alternatively, the 'cow-ness' of the cow-universal is simply the form (suti) of the word 'go'. In examples such as 'diṭṭhattaṃ' and 'diṭṭhanāmattaṃ', one should understand in this same manner.
34:
166. When compounds (samāsa), derivatives (taddhita), and primary derivatives (kita) occur in the sense of a universal (jāti) by way of convention (rūḷhī), suffixes such as -ṇya occur only in the sense of the universal. They do not occur in meanings such as relation (sambandha).

167. Whether words like 'sukka' (white) have a nature where quality and substance are undifferentiated, or whether they end in a derivative suffix, or whether they denote quality alone, those words occur in quality or in universal as appropriate.

168. Although the word 'santa' (being/existing) occurs in the sense of substance, action, and quality, it occurs because of a relation that is inseparable or because of an action.

169. We consider that 'assakaṇṇattaṃ', 'rājapuriisattaṃ', 'hatthittaṃ', 'daṇḍittaṃ', 'kumbhakārattaṃ', and 'gottaṃ' are the examples we intend.

170. The same applies to 'pācakattaṃ', the 'sukkattaṃ' of a cloth or the 'sukkattaṃ' of a quality, the 'sattā' (existence) of an evident object, 'kammaññaṃ', and 'devatā'.
35:
171. Although the etymology (byuppatti) through the analytical meaning (vigraha-vacanattha) may arise from any cause, the determination of meaning must be made only through established convention (rūḷhī). Thus, the meaning is determined by well-known convention, while the etymology can be formed by any suitable reason.

172. Those compounds, derivatives, verbs, and primary derivatives which, mostly due to the power of reference (apekkhaṇa-satti), occur in meanings such as the agent (kattā), are called 'utta' (expressed) meanings. Those which do not denote those meanings due to the absence of that power of reference are called 'anutta' (unexpressed) meanings.

173. A word that refers to an internal meaning along with an external meaning is called 'anutta' (unexpressed) based on that meaning. A word that refers to an external meaning along with an internal meaning should be noted as 'utta' (expressed).

174. "Who is the one with an excellent appearance by way of a beautiful form? That person is a man." "The man who has wealth by way of grain." "The cook cooks rice," or "The rice was cooked." These are like the given examples.

175. Grammatical rules (sutta) are pointed out as instructions for the sake of the successful accomplishment of usages like 'abhirūpo'. Therefore, the possessive (sāmī) and the seven cases (kāraka) are the places of origin (sañjātidesa) of the four great types of expressive words like compounds. Because of this, those possessives and cases are called 'utta' (expressed).
36:
176. The Sāmī (possessor) and the seven Kārakas (grammatical roles) which constitute the Jāti-khetta (field of birth), Āṇā-khetta (field of authority), and Visaya-khetta (field of scope) are called 'utta' (expressed). Due to the absence of these fields, they are called 'anutta' (unexpressed). This has been stated in the Jātinirutti text by the wise who understand 'utta' and 'anutta'.

177. In the Dispensation (Sāsana), the Jāti-khetta consists of ten thousand world-systems. The Āṇā-khetta consists of one hundred thousand crores of world-systems. The Visaya-khetta consists of infinite world-systems. Thus has the Buddha taught.

178. Because the indicators (vācaka) such as 'aṃ' are prescribed for those Sāmī and seven Kārakas, by worldly convention (saṅketa) alone, those indicators are called 'utta' (expressed) as they express that meaning. This is stated in the Kārikā text by a scholar proficient in Kārikā.

179. Some teachers say that only the major indicators such as Samāsa (compounds) express the meaning (utta), while the vibhatti (case endings) such as 'aṃ' do not (no utta). It is our (the author Saddhammasirī's) view that words which depend on the meaning are appropriate to be called expressed (utta), while those that do not depend on it are inappropriate.

180. The actual forms of the expressed (utta) and unexpressed (anutta) meanings are the seven Kārakas along with Bhāva (state) and Sāmī (relation). The case endings such as 'aṃ' and words such as Samāsa are the indicators (vācaka) that express them accordingly.
37:
181. Who is the one who conquered Māra? He is the Buddha (Jina). One who learns Abhidhamma is a monk (bhikkhu). The cook cooks rice; the cook is the one who cooks (pācaka). These are examples in the sense of the agent (kattā).

182. Those indicators such as Samāsa and vibhatti express only the sense of the agent (kattā) and the sense of possession (sāmī) directly. They do not express other meanings directly. They follow the primary meaning without contradicting it. They do not function in any other way than following the primary meaning.

183. Some teachers say that Samāsa and others express the meaning as indicators (vācaka). However, in their view, the designation 'agent' (kattā) etc. should apply to case endings like 'nā' and indicators like Samāsa. But in words like 'Jina', the designation 'agent' would not apply.

184. Therefore, only if Samāsa and other indicators are expressed as illuminators (jotaka), the designation 'agent' etc. is appropriate for words like 'Jina'. This is because when Samāsa etc. express a general meaning (sāmañña), the qualifier (visesana) like 'Jino' becomes meaningful.

185. Whether the Kāraka like 'Jina' is expressed by Samāsa etc. or not, it remains that Kāraka (agent etc.). There is no change from those Kārakas. Therefore, when words like 'Jina' are expressed by Samāsa etc., the name 'Kattu-kāraka' (agent role) etc. should occur.
38:
186. Indeed, indicators like Samāsa express a general meaning (sāmañña). A word ending in 'syādi' (case endings) expresses a specific meaning (visesa). Therefore, the word with a general meaning (such as 'jitamāro') is specified by the word with a specific meaning (such as 'jino').

187. Because the meanings of indicators like Samāsa have characteristics distinct from a sentence (vākya), the specific (visesa) meaning cannot be known by that sentence.

188. The word 'jitamāro' etc. is known to be general because it is used in conjunction with a qualifier like 'bhikkhu'. The word 'jina' etc. is also known to be general because it is used with a qualifier like 'katakicca' (one who has performed his duty). This is like the terms 'pāra' (the far shore) and 'apāra' (this shore).

189. Although the status of qualifier (visesana) and qualified (visesya) can occur according to the speaker's wish, people in the world understand the qualifier and qualified status based on what is well-known in worldly usage.

190. A word with a well-known meaning is called 'anuvāda-rūpa'. That anuvāda-rūpa is the qualifier (visesana). A word with a meaning that is not well-known is called 'vidhi-rūpa'.

191. That vidhi-rūpa is the qualified (visesya). Thus, words with meaning should be known as being of two kinds. Examples are 'nīluppalaṃ' (blue lotus) and 'rājapuriso' (king's man).
39:
191. Words with meaning are known to be of two kinds. A word with a well-known meaning (visesana) is called 'anuvāda-rūpa', and a word with a meaning not yet well-known (visesya) is called 'vidhi-rūpa'. Examples: "nīluppalaṃ" (blue lotus), "rājapuriso" (king's man).

192. If it is asked: "Since Samāsa etc. have already expressed the sense of the agent etc., should the case ending (vibhatti) not occur because it has no meaning of its own to express?" The answer is: Because it is impossible to indicate meaning without a case ending, the nominative case (paṭhamā vibhatti) occurs merely in consideration of the meaning of the stem (liṅgattha).

193. Even in the expressed sense of the agent etc., other cases like the instrumental (tatiyā) occur accordingly only when they depend on other actions (kriyā) etc.

194. The gender (liṅga), number (saṅkhyā), and case ending (vibhatti) seen in the qualified (visesya) should generally be made the same in the qualifier (visesana) when they have the same referent (tulyādhikaraṇa).

195. A word with a fixed gender and fixed singular number can only take the case ending of the primary qualified word. As in the example: "jāyanti cittāni vīsati" (twenty thoughts arise).
40:
196. Since a finite verb (ākhyāta) has no gender, it cannot follow the gender of the qualified (visesya). Therefore, only the number (saṅkhyā) remains the same as the qualified, due to its dependence on it.

197. Although the finite verb primarily expresses the meaning of action (kriyā), a Taddhita (secondary derivative) has the power to express the substance (dabba) of the word; thus, it primarily expresses the substance that possesses the power.

198. Because there is no power to express many Kārakas at the same moment, a finite verb or a Kita (primary derivative) expresses only one Kāraka at a time.

199. Whether expressed or unexpressed, a Kāraka is used because it is the cause of the action and its support. Indeed, every Kāraka is the cause for obtaining the action.

200. In the instrumental case (karaṇa-kāraka), there are many Samāsa and Kita forms such as 'chinna-rukkho' (the axe that cuts the tree) and 'paharaṇaṃ' (the weapon for striking). Taddhita forms like 'dutiyo' (the second) and 'gottaṃ' (lineage) are few.

201. In the accusative case (kamma-kāraka), examples of Samāsa, Taddhita, Ākhyāta, and Kita include: 'āgata-saṅgho' (the place where the Saṅgha has come), 'saṅghiko viဟာရော' (the monastery belonging to the Saṅgha), 'ghātiko odano' (rice mixed with ghee), 'paccate odano' (rice is cooked), and 'pacito odano' (rice has been cooked).

202. In the example 'bhujjate odano' (rice is eaten), the word 'odana' is expressed in its primary sense (mukhya). In the example 'paccate odano' (rice is cooked), it is expressed in a non-primary sense (amukhya) due to the metaphorical use of the name of the result (phala-nāmūpacāra).
41:
201. In the objective case (kamma-kāraka), what is meant by "āgatasangho" (the place where the Sangha arrives)? That place is indeed a monastery belonging to the Sangha. "Ghātiko odano" refers to rice mixed with ghee. "Odano paccate" means rice is cooked; "pacito odano" means cooked rice.

202. In the example "odano bhujjate" (rice is eaten), the word 'odana' is used in its literal sense (mukhya). However, in the example "odano paccate" (rice is cooked), it is used in a non-literal sense through metonymy (phalanāmūpacāra), where the name of the effect (cooked rice) is attributed to the cause (raw rice).

203. When a verb with a single object expresses the object, that single object is known as the expressed object (vutta-kamma). When a verb with multiple objects expresses an object, which among those objects is to be known as the expressed object (vutta-kamma)?

204. Among the multiple objects of roots belonging to the Duha group (duhádi), the secondary object (appadhāna-kamma) is known as the expressed object (vutta-kamma). However, among the multiple objects of roots belonging to the Nī group (nayādi), the primary object (padhāna-kamma) is known as the expressed object (vutta-kamma).

205. Roots such as duha, yāca, rudhi, puccha, bhikkha, sāsa, and vaca, as well as roots such as nī, vaha, and hara—both these types of roots possess two objects each (dvikammika).
42:
206. "The cowherd milks the cow for milk," or "The cowherd milks the milk from the cow." (The wise) have said, "The milk is milked from the cow by the cowherd," or "The cow is milked for milk by the cowherd."

207. "The goat-herd leads the goat to the village," or "The goat-herd leads the goat to the village." (It is also said), "The goat is led to the village by the goat-herd," or "The goat is led to the village by the goat-herd."

208. The object that is most intended by the action, such as milking or leading, is called the primary object (padhāna-kamma). The object that serves merely as the occasion for the action is called the secondary object (appadhāna-kamma).

209. That object which the agent desires through the action is the primary object (padhāna-kamma). That which is the opposite of the desired object (not specifically intended) is known as the secondary object (appadhāna-kamma).

210. It is stated in the Jātinirutti text that the primary and secondary objects are the domain (visaya) of verbs (ākhyāta) and primary derivatives (kita) according to established usage.

211. In a non-causative sentence involving roots meaning going, knowing, eating, or making sound, as well as the roots hara, kara, and intransitive roots, the agent (kattā) that exists there is to be regarded as the expressed object (vutta-kamma) in a causative sentence.
43:
211. In a non-causative sentence, the simple agent (suddha-kattā) of roots meaning going, knowing, eating, or making sound, as well as the roots hara, kara, and intransitive roots like 'sī' (to sleep), is to be understood as the expressed object (vutta-kamma) in a causative sentence.

212. "The servant goes to the village" is a non-causative sentence. In a causative sentence, it becomes: "The master makes the servant go to the village."

213. "The elephant sleeps" is a non-causative sentence of an intransitive root. In a causative sentence, it becomes: "The mahout makes the elephant sleep." This principle also applies to primary derivatives (kita).

214. Although it is the agent of the result-action (phala-kriyā), it is considered an object (kamma) because of its connection to the causative action (hetu-kriyā). This is because it cannot be established as an agent in any other way than through the status of an object.

215. When another instigating agent (payojaka-kattā) commands a simple agent (suddha-kattā), a causative suffix (kārita) is added after the root. Similarly, if there is a further instigation of the instigating agent, another causative suffix is added again after the root that already ends in a causative suffix.
44:
216. It should be known that according to the preference of grammarians, this causative suffix can be applied up to three levels. When applied in two or three levels, the preceding causative suffix is always elided by the rule of nipātanā.

217. The cook cooks the rice. The head cook makes the assistant cook the rice. Similarly, it should be noted that a minister or a king makes the rice and other objects be cooked.

218. The cook cooks; he causes to cook. The head cook makes the assistant cook the rice, using either the instrumental, accusative, or genitive case for the assistant. The minister and the king are understood in the same way.

219. When connected with the causative action (hetu-kriyā) meaning 'to cause', the status of being an object is understood. This is because the causative action is primary, and it cannot reach the status of an agent other than through the status of an object.

220. However, when connected with the result-action (phala-kriyā) such as 'to cook', the status of being an agent is understood according to the provision of the word 'vā' (optionally). Apart from the accusative case, the status of an agent can be recognized in other cases like the instrumental and genitive.

221. Roots are classified as intransitive (akammaka), transitive with one object (ekakammaka), or transitive with two objects (dvikammaka) based on whether they naturally expect an object or not. Examples include the roots bhū, gamu, nī, etc.
45:
221. Roots are classified as intransitive (akammaka), transitive with one object (ekakammaka), or transitive with two objects (dvikammaka) based on whether they naturally expect an object or not. Examples include the roots bhū, gamu, nī, and so on.

222. A causative suffix (kārita) occurring with a root produces a single object. A prefix (upasagga) occurring with a root also makes it transitive or intransitive as appropriate.

223. Because a specific meaning becomes clear in roots combined with causative suffixes and prefixes, these suffixes and prefixes illuminate the already existing meaning, just as a lamp illuminates objects.

224. (The monk) develops wholesome Dhamma. (The people) make the monk go on the path. The wealthy man enjoys wealth. The sun rises.

225. The king to whom tax is given, the Arahant monk who is worthy of offerings, and the Brahmin to whom a gift is given are examples in the dative case (sampadāna-kāraka). The village from which the villager has departed is an example in the ablative case (apādāna).
46:
226. The village from which the villager departs, or the village that is the source of the villager's departure, and the cause of origin—these are examples in the ablative case (apādāna-kāraka). In a subtle form of the ablative case, 'gotta' (the genus/class of 'cow'), which is the source of the cognition of the word 'cow', is also an example. In the locative case (okāsa-kāraka), a village with abundant paddy is an example.

227. A forest with trees and a house as a dwelling are examples in the locative case (okāsa-kāraka). Since the finite verb (ākhyāta) does not express the four cases starting with the instrumental (karaṇa), the group of four cases starting with karaṇa is not illustrated in the context of ākhyāta.

228. Because its range of expression is narrow, the verbal signifier (ākhyāta-vācaka) expresses only the three cases: state (bhāva), object (kamma), and agent (kattā). Because its range of expression is broad, the participial signifier (kita-vācaka) expresses the seven cases including state (bhāva).

229. 'Gotta' (cow-ness), which is the source of the cognition of the word 'cow', and the actions of the cook such as staying (ṭhīyate) or cooking (pacanaṃ), are examples of the stative sense (bhāva-vācaka). This is understood because the suffixes are prescribed in the sense of bhāva. Where the rule for compounds (samāsa) is not prescribed for the sense of bhāva, it is not illustrated as an example in the context of compounds.

230. The abstract sense in derivative nouns (taddhita-bhāva) occurs in the senses of substance (dabba), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), name (nāma), and genus (jāti). The abstract sense in finite verbs (ākhyāta-bhāva) and primary derivatives (kita-bhāva) occurs only in the sense of action (kriyā). This is the distinction between taddhita-bhāva and the bhāva of ākhyāta and kita.
47:
231. The ākhyāta-bhāva (verbal abstract) has the meaning of the action which is the sense of the root; it does not have two numbers (it has only the singular); it does not have the three genders; and it does not mix with other kārakas (grammatical roles) other than the three kārakas of bhāva (abstract), kamma (object), and kattar (agent). The kit-bhāva (derivative abstract), however, exists with the three genders and with the two numbers. These are the distinctions between ākhyāta-bhāva and kit-bhāva.

232. "The Buddha who possesses the ten powers" (Dasabalo), "The lute-player who possesses the skill of playing the lute" (Veṇiko)—these are examples of the sense of relation (sambandha) in compounds (samāsa) and secondary derivatives (taddhita). That sense of relation is not cited as an example for ākhyāta and kit because it is not expressed by them.

233. "The Buddha who has conquered Māra" (Jitamāro), "The sword which is the cause of cutting the tree" (Chinnarukkho), "The village to which the villagers have come" (Āgatagāmiko), "The soldier to whom wealth has been given" (Dinnadhano), "The house from which the householder has departed" (Nikkhantagahito).

234. In the example "The village which has abundant paddy" (Sampannavīhi gāmo), the six kārakas are expressed by means of a compound (samāsa). It should also be understood that relation (sambandha) is expressed in "The Lord Buddha who is the refuge and possesses the ten powers" (Dasabalo Nātho).

235. In a Bahubbīhi compound where there is an external sense (aññapadattha), if the quality or attribute is known through the sense of that external word, or by the power of its association with that external sense, that Bahubbīhi compound is called Tadguṇa-bahubbīhi. A Bahubbīhi compound with an external sense that is not known in that manner is called Atadguṇa-bahubbīhi.
48:
236. "This man with a severed hand (Chinnahattho) is known," "The man with a blue cloth (Nīlapaṭo) is a human." "The Saṅgha headed by the Buddha" (Sambuddhappamukho Saṅgho), "The man who has seen the ocean" (Diṭṭhasāgaro)—these are also examples.

237. Because the words 'ca', 'ta', etc., which indicate the sense of aggregation (samuccaya) in Dvanda compounds, and the sense of equality (tulya) in Digu and Kammadhāraya compounds, are not seen, those senses of aggregation and equality are expressed [by the compounds themselves]. They do not express the kārakas, nor do they express relation (sambandha).

238. Avyayībhāva and Amādi-tappurisa compounds express the sense of relation (sambandha) together with the kāraka. This is understood by inferring the hint (lesa) which is the elision (lopa) of the case endings that indicate those kāraka and sambandha meanings.

239. Non-compounding occurs because of dependence on a word other than those suitable for compounding. Other scholars say that non-compounding occurs because of dependence on a word that is separated by another word.

240. "The black teeth of Devadatta" (Devadattassa kaṇhadantā), "The King's man, cows, and horses" (Rañño puriso gavo asso ca)—these examples will be discussed regarding how compounding can occur without considering the state of dependence (on an external word).
49:
241. Once the state of having a common substratum (Kammadhāraya) and the state of having the sense of 'ca' (Dvanda) have been formed, even if there is dependence on that word, the established compound does not perish. Furthermore, Amādi-tappurisa compounds and others also occur.

242. In these examples: "The King's horse" (Rājasso), "One possessing form" (Rūpavā), "One pierced by an arrow" (Sallaviddho), "Cow" (Go)—even if there is dependence on another word, they attain the status of a compound because they are principal (padhāna). However, a compound cannot be formed due to the dependence of a non-principal (appadhāna) word;

243. Yet, if there is gamaka-satti (the power to convey the meaning), the status of a compound can indeed exist in a compound just as it does in a sentence.

244. In examples such as "Devadatta's teacher's family" (Devadattassa gurukulaṃ), the connection of the word 'Devadattassa' occurs first by reaching (connecting with) the component part (aṅga) which is 'guru', and only afterwards with the whole (aṅgī) which is 'gurukulaṃ'.

245. A word such as 'na', which has a connection in meaning only with a word such as 'geyya', should be compounded with a word such as 'puna'. That compound is to be known as Ayuttattha-samāsa (a compound with improper connection).
50:
246. Generally, because the rule (sutta) "a compound has a unified meaning" (samāso yuttattho) is stated, [Ayuttattha-samāsa must be explained]. Alternatively, if a word such as 'puna' is first combined [with 'geyya'] and afterwards the word 'na' is combined [with 'punageyya'], then that compound is called Yuttattha-samāsa in examples such as 'apunageyyā'.

247. Negation (paṭisedha) is of two kinds: Pasajja-paṭisedha, which is marked by the non-existence of the thing being prohibited, and Pariyudāsa, which is marked by a thing similar to the thing being prohibited.

248. Being associated with wrong knowledge, a word often expresses the meanings of non-existence (abhāva) and similarity (tulyatā). Therefore, these compounds "akattvāna" and "abrāhmaṇa" are Yuttattha-samāsa.

249. A compound is of one kind by way of condensing words. Alternatively, it is of two kinds by way of sound-compound (sadda-samāsa) and meaning-compound (attha-samāsa), or by way of elided (lutta) and non-elided (alutta) compounds.

250. A compound is also of two kinds by way of permanent (nicca) and non-permanent (anicca) compounds. Alternatively, it is of three kinds by way of the elision of the initial, middle, or final words.
51:
251. "One who has wealth in the form of cattle" (Godhano), "One who has hair on the chest" (Urasilomo), "One who makes pots" (Kumbhakāro)—these are examples as appropriate. The examples "Datto" (from Devadatto), "Assaratho" (horse-chariot), and "Rūpaṃ" (from Rūpabhava), etc., are respectively examples of initial-word elision (ādipada-lopa), middle-word elision (majjhepada-lopa), and final-word elision (uttarapada-lopa).

252. In examples such as "Assaratho", the verb is no longer seen because of the elision of the final word "yutta" (joined), or because of the mutual dependence between the kāraka "assa" (horse) and the action "yutta", or because the compound has already expressed [the sense of the action 'joined', etc.].

253. It should be understood as appropriate that compounds are of four types based on the prominence (padhāna) of the meaning: initial-word prominence, final-word prominence, both-words prominence, or external-word prominence.

254. In another way, compounds are of six types: Avyayībhāva, Tulyādhikaraṇa (Kammadhāraya), Digu, Tappurisa, Dvanda, and Bāhirattha (Bahubbīhi).

255. For example: "Near the city" (Upanagaraṃ) means the vicinity of that city. "Blue lotus" (Nīluppalaṃ) means the lotus. "Three factors" (Tiyaṅgaṃ) means the factors. "The King's horse" (Rājasso) means the horse. "One with a severed hand" (Chinnakaro) means the person.
52:
256. A scholar who knows the methods of compounding should understand that these five types of compound meanings possess qualifiers (visesana). In particular, the two meanings in "Samaṇabrāhmaṇā" (ascetics and brahmins) are meanings of a single term and do not have qualifiers.

257. The relationship of qualifier and qualified (visesana-visesya) exists in compounds excluding the Dvanda compound. In the Dvanda compound, that state does not exist; therefore, is it not true that the state of unified meaning (ekatthībhāva) is inappropriate for Dvanda terms like 'Samaṇabrāhmaṇā'?

258. Only in the case of a Dvanda compound, words occurring with the particle 'ca' (ca-nipāta) primarily express their own meaning, and the particle 'ca' also indicates another meaning; it cannot indicate it in any other way.

259. Therefore, some teachers say that unified meaning (ekatthībhāva) also occurs in Dvanda compounds. Other teachers say that unified meaning occurs because of the commonality of connection to a single verb.

260. Words that do not depend on each other merely by their connection to a verb act as if they are dependent. Therefore, it is accepted that the state of unified meaning (ekatthatā) occurs because of the subsequent verb which has an undivided meaning.
53: 261. In the use of Taddhita (derivative) terms, examples include: a monk learned in the Abhidhamma, the fifth letter, food mixed with ghee, and an Arahant (Brahmana) worthy of receiving offerings. 262. Similarly, in examples such as the breed of cattle, a place with trees, and a man who plays the lute, the Taddhita term denotes only the substantive (visesya) due to its association with suffixes like vāṇa and others. 263. Handiwork performed by a servant, a man who crosses by boat, a monk who recites the Abhidhamma, merit performed for the sake of heaven, a small river flowing from a mountain, 264. bodily feeling, and the son of Vasiṭṭha—in such examples, the Taddhita term denotes the adjective (visesana). It is stated that this denotes the adjective because the teacher Kaccāyana included the word "vā" in the rule "yenavā saṃsappaṃ" etc. 265. This Taddhita is of three types: Sāmañña-taddhita, Avyaya-taddhita, and Bhāva-taddhita. Taddhita suffixes such as ṇa and others arise only after the first word that ends in a case-ending.
54: 266. Vāsiṭṭho, sabbathā, and pācakattaṃ are examples (of Sāmañña, Avyaya, and Bhāva Taddhita respectively). Suffixes such as jja and to occur in the sense of case-endings. Some teachers say these suffixes occur in the sense of kāraka (grammatical roles) and so on. 267. In the sense of "the son of Vasiṭṭha," suffixes such as ṇa that follow the first word ending in the genitive case can take both meanings (the base and the suffix). Suffixes that follow the word "apacca" (offspring) take only one meaning and cannot take both. 268. The abbreviation of words is called Samāsa (compounding), while a word together with a suffix is called Taddhita. Thus, one should note the difference between Samāsa and Taddhita. 269. Only suffixes such as ṇa are called Taddhita. Other scholars know that the process completed through mental reflection and so on is also called Taddhita. 270. A word that has many meanings through the mixture of different senses is called sahabbacanicchāvacana. In the context of a Dvanda (copulative compound), this sahabbacanicchāvacana word becomes ekasesa (one-remainder).
55: 271. In the Panini grammar (Timunisatthaka) composed by the three sages, it should be known that the teacher Dabbapadatthika employed ekasesa to make a single word when intending to express many meanings, for fear of wordiness. 272. In the Cāndra grammar, however, it is stated that just as the word "ahaṃ" expresses one meaning and "mayaṃ" expresses many meanings, and similarly, words like "puriso" express one meaning while "purisā" express many meanings, there is no need to employ ekasesa. 273. Although it is stated thus in the Cāndra grammar, since the commentators (Aṭṭhakathā) who knew the intention of the Lord of Sages (the Buddha) explained ekasesa in the commentaries and sub-commentaries, its characteristics should be noted at least briefly. 274. Some teachers say that ekasesa should be applied only to the stem (liṅga) before case-endings are attached, because there is no subsequent cause (nimitta). Other teachers who preserve the ancient tradition say that ekasesa should be applied only to words ending in case-endings. 275. Other scholars know ekasesa as the remaining of one from a group of identical-sounding words. Thus, three views are established in the Atthavyākhyāna.
56: 276. To indicate the state of having an identical kāraka, to make known an unknown meaning, and to show the expanded meaning of the analysis (vigraha), a word ending in a case-ending and the word "ca" (and) are employed. 277. Just as one cow may belong to four people, or as a single lamp can clearly illuminate all things, so too can multiple numbers be understood through a single case-ending. 278. Some teachers call that ekasesa a pure noun (nāma) because it lacks a suffix. Other teachers call it Taddhita through mental reflection, even though the suffix is absent. 279. Some teachers call it Taddhita, and others call it Dvanda compound. Because it lacks the characteristics of those (noun, Taddhita, or Dvanda), it should be noted by that very name as ekasesa. 280. The word "purisā" can be formed through the conception of ekasesa, or as a Kita (derivative) from "pūrenti" (they fill), or as an Upapada compound from "puriṭṭhāne senti" (they dwell in a noble place).
57: 281. In examples such as mātaro (mother and father), pitaro (mother and father), sāriputtā (Sāriputta and Moggallāna), and puttā (son and daughter), the ekasesa of words with different forms is stated by the method of yogavibhāga (splitting of a rule). 282. In examples such as mātaro, pitaro, and nāmarūpaṃ, either the preceding word, the succeeding word, or a part of them remains. 283. In examples such as nāmarūpaṃ, when the formation of ekasesa is complete, it also regards the general class (sāmaññajāta). Because it so regards it, the singular number (ekavacana) occurs. 284. Even in sarūpekasesa (ekasesa of identical forms), there are three varieties based on the nature of the word, the meaning, or both the word and meaning. The examples are māsā (months and beans), kuṭilā (crooked things), and purisā (men). 285. Among words uttered repeatedly, a word with many meanings is called vicchāvacana (vicchā word). A word with a single meaning that is uttered twice or thrice is called āmeḍita.
58: 286. In vicchā, the doubling (dvebhāva) of a single word with various meanings occurs due to nipātanā (special prescription). In āmeḍita, there is no doubling (in the same sense) because it has only one meaning and is used due to fear and so on. Some teachers, regarding the occurrence of such vicchā and āmeḍita, call āmeḍita "dvebhāva" as well because of its multiple forms. 287. Vicchā is understood as the speaker's desire to pervade objects that are distinct by way of substance, quality, or action. 288. As in the examples: "There is water in every village (gāme gāme)," "Every village is delightful," "Every village is known." In some vicchā such as "ekekaṃ," the elision of case-endings like "si" occurs. 289. Because it depends on another word and because it has two forms, there is no state of being a compound (samāsa) in vicchā. In the word "tadattho," however, there is compounding with the dependent word "attha." 290. In the examples: "The cook cooks rice," "Rice is cooked by that cook," "Devadatta stands," the verb (ākhyāta) expresses the three kārakas.
59:
291. The meaning of a root that is pure and unmixed with functional roles (kārakas) is to be understood as 'state' (bhāva). That state is an action (kriyā) and has a general (sāmañña) nature that is common to many. The oneness (singular number/ekattasaṅkhyā) of that general state is to be understood.

292. When it is that general action, the term expressing the state (bhāva) ends in the third person (paṭhamapurisa) singular suffix. However, sometimes the plural suffix may also occur when considering the plurality of agents (kattās) and so forth.

293. Just as in 'Sabbhi sambhūyate' (The virtuous ones exist well), where the singular occurs despite the plural agent; and just as in 'Āsīyante uṭṭhāsikā yathā bhavantehi' (As the camels sleep, so do the masters sleep), where the plural occurs in consideration of the plurality of agents; thus, in the expression of state (bhāva), the distinction or non-distinction of number may sometimes occur.

294. Regarding forms such as 'Pahīyissanti te' (Those things will be abandoned by themselves) and 'Rūpaṃ bhūyate' (Form arises by itself), although some teachers speak of them in the sense of the reflexive (kammakattā), the author of the Saddanīti, who knows those forms, speaks of them only in the sense of state (bhāva).

295. In the Saddanīti, it is stated that the nominative case (paccatta) is applied to the agent of a verb expressing state (bhāva). Another teacher firmly asserts that this nominative case occurs only in the sense of the agent of the instrumental case.
60:
296. A word ending in the nominative, such as 'rūpaṃ', stands in consideration of the mere meaning of the stem (liṅgattha) as distinguished by the agent and so forth. That nominative-ended word is sometimes understood in a way that does not conflict with the speaker's intention (vatticchā).

297. After a transitive root (sakammaka), the verbal suffixes (ākhyātapaccaya) occur in the sense of the agent (kattā) and the object (kamma), but not in the sense of state (bhāva). After an intransitive root (akammaka), however, they occur in the sense of the agent and the state, but not in the sense of the object.

298. When there is no desire to express the object, verbal suffixes may occur in the sense of state (bhāva) even after a transitive root. An example is: 'Devadattena gehe paccate' (There is cooking by Devadatta in the house).

299. The intention to speak (vatticchā) may not occur even for an existing thing, and it may occur even for a non-existing thing. Examples are: 'Anudarā kaññā' (A waistless maiden) and 'Samuddo kuṇḍikā' (The ocean is a water-pot) or 'Kuṇḍikā samuddo' (The water-pot is the ocean).

300. This is because the meanings of all roots have the nature of existence (sattā) and the nature of action (karaṇa). Therefore, because they are common to all roots, 'state' (bhāva) which is existence, and 'action' (kriyā) which is doing, are to be understood in the meanings of all roots.
61:
301. Since the terms 'bhāva' and 'kāraṇa' are general terms (sāmañña), it is appropriate to explain the meanings of all roots using these terms. For example, the word 'rukkha' (tree) can denote specific trees like 'dhava' (Anogeissus latifolia) and others.

302. However, specific (visesa) terms like 'pāka' (cooking) cannot explain the meanings of all roots. This is like how the word 'palāsa' (Butea frondosa) and others cannot denote all trees.

303. Since an adverb (kriyāvisesana) stands in the sense of the agent or the object, it is established by logical reasoning. Therefore, no separate rule (sutta) is stated for the sake of the adverb.

304. In the phrase 'Muduṃ pacati' (He cooks softly), the meaning is 'Pacanā bhavati' (Cooking occurs [softly]). In the phrase 'Sukhaṃ sayati' (He sleeps happily), the meaning is 'Sayanaṃ karoti' (He performs sleeping [happily]).

305. Just as the word 'kamma' occurs in the sense of the object, so it also occurs in the sense of state (bhāva/action). Alternatively, by means of the retention of one (ekasesa) or the lamp method (padīpanaya), the application of the accusative case in an adverb is stated by the rule 'kammatthe'.
62:
306. In treatises such as the Bālāvatarā and Sambandhacintā, that which is neuter and ends in the accusative singular is called an adverb having that state (taggati).

307. It is stated in the Atthabyākhyāna that if one considers the unity of the components (the action and the adverb), the nominative case (paṭhamā) should occur. If one considers the distinction in meaning, the accusative case (dutiyā) should occur.

308. When one considers the non-distinction and identity between the action being qualified (visesya) and the adverb (visesana), then the nominative case occurs in this adverb because it is the mere meaning of the stem (liṅgattha).

309. When one considers the distinction (between the adverb and the action), then the accusative case occurs because it is a part of that action. Since that action has the nature of oneness, it should always be in the singular number.

310. Because it does not have the nature of being an auxiliary (constituent) to the agent, it is not an instrumental functional role (karaṇakāraka). For this very reason, wise men who know adverbs also recognize adverbs that end in the instrumental case (tatiyā).
63:
311. Other wise men know the adverb as ending in the genitive case (chaṭṭhī). Examples are: 'Ekāheneva pāyāsi' (He went in just one day) and 'Pādassukkhipanaṃ' (The lifting of the foot).

312. In Sanskrit grammar, the adverb is called 'qualifier of the root' (dhātuvisesana). In the Dispensation (Commentarial) texts, however, that adverb is well-described as 'neuter of state' (bhāvanapuṃsaka).

313. It is well-stated that there are two kinds of adverbs. All vocative words (ālapana) are called external adverbs (bahiddhākriyāvisesana). Words such as 'muduṃ' (softly) are called internal adverbs (abahiddhākriyāvisesana).

314. That action which has been undertaken to be accomplished but has not yet reached completion is called the present (vattamāna). That same present action is also called incomplete (vippakata).

315. When there is an interruption in the continuity of action, it is called the past (atīta). When the action has not yet been undertaken, it is called the future (anāgata). In this way, the triad of time is marked by action.
64:
316. That meaning of a word which is without beginning or end, eternal, and does not arise due to causes, and which is always shown, is known as 'Time' (kāla) by those who know time.

317. Just as space (ākāsa), though one and eternal, is divided into 'space in a pot' and so forth due to its association with substances like a pot, so also time, though one and undivided, is divided into many.

318. Although time is of one kind, it is divided by the metaphorical attribution of the division of actions to time. Although action is of one kind, it is divided only because of the division of agents and so forth.

319. Although action is undivided in its general state, it is divided by place and so forth. Therefore, other wise men say that there is the retention of one (ekasesa) in verbs (ākhyāta).

320. The division of action is understood only through the division of agents and so forth; it is not understood through the retention of one (ekasesa). Thus, it is prohibited in the Nyāsa and other treatises.
65:
321. In the context of what is expressed (vutta) by verbal terminations (ākhyāta-vibhatti), the Second Person (majjhima-purisa) occurs due to association with the word tumha (you). The First Person (uttama-purisa) occurs due to association with the word amha (I). The Third Person (paṭhama-purisa) occurs due to association with other nouns remaining after tumha and amha. However, this does not occur in the context of what is not expressed (avutta).

322. Due to association with suffixes such as āya which express the meaning of the root, [the word] abandons its nature as a noun and stands only in the nature of a root (dhātu).

323. It is evident as 'having an agent' or 'having an object' through the agent and object of the root-meaning expressed by the suffix such as āya. Therefore, such a word is called 'root-form' (dhāturūpa).

324. There are examples such as "The Sangha acts like a mountain" (pabbatāyati) and "He treats the child as shaven-headed" (bālaṃ muṇḍāyati). Because it makes known the object bālaṃ, the word muṇḍa, which has expectancy (sāpekkha), is used in association with the expected word bāla.

325. When intending to express a name, a verbal form (ākhyāta) becomes a nominal form associated with nominal case-endings. Such examples as Mākhali and others have been cited in the Saddanīti treatise.
66:
326. Other scholars know the sādhana (mode of derivation) such as the agent (kattu) as upaggaha. Some teachers say the qualifier (visesana) of that sādhana is upaggaha. The inclusion of that upaggaha is within the kāraka (grammatical relation).

327. Although the root expresses the action, because the verbal meaning of the root, which usually occurs not without terminations and suffixes, is evident in the ākhyāta (verb), and

328. Because it expresses action with the predominance of action (kriyā-padhāna), it is called ākhyāta. Some teachers say it is called ākhyāta because it expresses the action, which is the meaning of the root, by way of metaphorical attribution (upacāra) [to the agent or object].

329. This action is evident through contradictory statements such as "I go" and "I do not go." Alternatively, this action is evident through questions such as "What are you doing?" and the answer "I am cooking."

330. Thus, because the agent and object have the nature of being accomplished (sādhya-rūpa), the predominance of action is understood only in the ākhyāta. In the kita (primary derivative), the predominance of substance (dabba-padhāna) is understood because it has an established nature (siddha-rūpa).
67:
331. One who cooks is pācaka. One who cooks rice is bhattakāra. An instrument for striking is paharaṇa, such as a sword. That which is cooked is paccita, which is rice. The person to whom something is given is dānīya, such as a monk. The place where something originates is pabhava, such as the Himālaya.

332. A place for sitting, such as a couch or a stool, is āsana. The act of standing is ṭhāna. Thus, the kita expresses seven sādhanas, with bhāva (abstract state) being the seventh.

333. It should be understood that sādhana is of seven types: kattu-sādhana (agent), karaṇa-sādhana (instrument), kamma-sādhana (object), sampadāna-sādhana (recipient), avadhi-sādhana (ablative, also called apādāna), adhikaraṇa-sādhana (locative), and bhāva-sādhana (state/action).

334. Bhāva-sādhana is the meaning of the root unmixed with kārakas. That root-meaning is the action. If the root expresses the root-meaning, for what purpose are the terminations and suffixes applied?

335. According to the rule "Neither bases (roots and stems) nor suffixes are used alone," terminations and suffixes are applied because of the expectancy for the bhāva-sādhana (the abstract meaning of the action).
68:
336. Due to the power of the words—the kita suffix and the ākhyāta termination—bhāva (state/action) is divided into two types: siddha-bhāva (accomplished state) and sādhya-bhāva (state to be accomplished). It is stated in the Atthavyākhyāna that the examples are pāka (cooking) and ṭhīyati (he stands), respectively.

337. Just as a single person can be known as an uncle and also as a teacher, similarly, bhāva is known as 'action' (kriyā) due to the base root, and as 'sādhana' due to the suffix and termination.

338-339. The action-substance (kriyā-dabba) which possesses kāraka force is called bhāva. In that case, when associated with that action-substance, the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) occurs in the sense of possession (sāmī). However, when the meaning of the root is expected, the instrumental case (tatiyā) occurs in the sense of the agent (kattu). Some teachers say the genitive case is like a hook (lākhūpamā), or that it is an adverbial qualifier (kriyā-visesana) ending in the genitive case due to association with that root.

340. Just as distinction is attributed to the non-existent (abhāva) or space (ākāsa), which have no inherent distinctions, due to the distinction of the related substances (sambandhī-dabba), similarly, distinction is attributed to the action (bhāva), which has no inherent distinction, due to the distinction of the related substances. Its inherent lack of distinction should also be understood.
69:
341. In the kita-bhāva, one can say "the cookings of oil, ghee, etc." (plural) or "the cooking occurs" (singular). In the ākhyāta-bhāva, however, the genitive case cannot occur in the sense of possession (sāmī-lakkhaṇa) because the genitive case is not suitable to be associated with it.

342. Just as a kāraka such as a mat (kaṭa), which supports the agent etc. who are the locus of the action, is called the support (ādhāra) of the action, the same applies to the agent-substance which is the locus of that action.

343. Even for the non-manifest bhāva (action), the designation 'agent' (kattu) is mentioned in the Saddanīti. This is said because this kita-bhāva becomes differentiated due to the differentiation of substances such as the agent.

344. Because it is the object of conventional usage, because the substance (dabba) is predominant in the kita, and because it is understood like a substance, the scholars who know the kita-bhāva call it a 'substance' (dabba).

345. A specific action (visesa-kriyā) qualified by the universal of action (kriyā-jāti), which is the cause for the application of the word (sadda-pavattinimitta), is called a 'substance' (dabba). When there is another verb such as "they are" (honti), the manifestation of forces (satti) such as the agent appears.

346. It is called kita because it dispels the doubts of students. Because kita suffixes occur frequently, it is called the Kitaka (the treatise on kita).
70:
346. It dispels [doubts], therefore it is called kita. The meaning is that it dispels the doubts of students. Because kita suffixes occur frequently, it is called the Kitaka treatise.

347. In the Kitaka treatise, suffixes are of two types: kicca suffixes and kita suffixes. The five suffixes starting with tabba are called kicca suffixes. Other suffixes starting with ṇa are kita suffixes.

348. Suffixes are of three types: kicca, kita, and kicca-kita. Other scholars know that they occur in the sense of the state (bhāva), the object (kamma), the agent (kattu), or in all three.

349. After intransitive roots (akammaka-dhātu), kicca suffixes occur only in the sense of the state (bhāva) in the neuter gender. After transitive roots (sakammaka-dhātu), they mostly occur in the sense of the object (kamma), and those words ending in such suffixes possess all three genders.

350. Kita suffixes should be understood to be in the sense of the agent (kattu); this statement is merely an illustration (upalakkhaṇa). Therefore, kicca and kita suffixes may occur in the senses of agent, object, state, and so on.
71:
351. In the *Nyāsa* treatise, those suffixes beginning with *ṇa* and ending with *yu* are marked by the rule "*ṇādayo tekālikā*"; those suffixes are said to be associated with the three periods of time. However, those suffixes not marked by the rule are said to be suffixes free from the three times, or suffixes associated with one, two, or three periods of time.

352. Other suffixes whose time is not indicated by their respective rules are not marked by time. It is stated in the *Rūpasiddhi* treatise that only those suffixes whose time is indicated by their respective rules are marked by time.

353. Although those suffixes beginning with *ṇa* and ending with *yu* are associated with the three times, in forms such as *Purindada*, they occur only in the past tense due to the meaning of the proximate word (*upapada*) "*pure*". Some teachers say they occur in the present tense.

354. Although there is a distinction through many different lives, the present tense (*vattamāna*) is used in the *Buddhavaṃsa* Commentary and others, based on the oneness of the individual continuum (*santāna*).

355. Alternatively, in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*, the present tense is used because of considering that current moment of occurrence. In the *Jātaka* Commentary, however, the past tense is used by considering an existence other than this present existence where the Buddha appeared.
72:
356. "Now Devadatta was the hunter at that time (the time of the Chaddanta Jātaka)." "At that time (the time of realizing the Four Noble Truths), I (the Buddha) dwell (at the Bodhi tree)." "At that time (four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons ago), I, being Sumedha, went through the sky."

357. Because the past and the future are dependent on the present moment, it is therefore appropriate to form a three-timed derivative (*tekālika-viggaha*) at a single moment.

358. There are past and future parts that occur before and after a certain present moment. Based on that present moment, a suffix is understood as occurring in the three times. Why? Because the occurrence of words is dependent on the speaker's intention.

359. The status of being an agent (*kattu*) of past and future actions can exist either because the capacity of the present action is metaphorically attributed to the agent of the past or future action, or because the agent is suitable to perform those past and future actions.

360. Just as one is called a 'cook' (*pācaka*) because of being suitable for cooking even if not currently cooking, likewise, the status of being an agent can exist because of being suitable for the action even if not currently acting.
73:
361. The wise one (Venerable Buddhappiya) who knows the characteristics of compounds has demonstrated in the *Rūpasiddhi* treatise that the augment *nu* comes only after eliding the case endings in the proximate word (*upapada*) because it is a compound (*samāsa*).

362. In the *Kaccāyana* and *Nyāsa* treatises, the status of being an unelided compound (*alutta-samāsa*) is stated in the section on compounds. However, in the section on primary derivatives (*kita*), the status of being an elided compound (*lutta-samāsa*) is stated precisely because of the arrival of the augment *nu*.

363. Although a suffix used in the sense of habit (*tassīla*), nature (*taddhamma*), or doing well (*tassādhukāritā*) is free from the seven kinds of grammatical instruments (*sādhana*), it is still a *kita* suffix because it occurs after a root and functions in the place of an agent.

364. Ancient teachers have included the meaning of such suffixes within the agentive instrument (*kattu-sādhana*). Habit (*sīla*), which is a natural disposition, is understood as the meaning of the root because it shares the same locus with the meaning of the word 'that' (*ta*).

365. Customary practice (*dhamma*), which is the conduct of the virtuous, is also understood as the meaning of the root. As for 'doing well' (*tassādhukāritā*), it is understood as 'acting with care' (*sakkaccakāritā*) within the meaning of that root, because it has a different locus from the meaning of the word 'that' (*ta*).
74:
366. To give examples: the form '*Kumbhakāro*' is shown for the three times; the form '*Dīpaṅkaro*' is shown for elided and unelided compounds; and the form '*Bhikkhu*' is shown for the sense of habit (*tassīla*) and others.

367. The genitive case (*chaṭṭhī*) sometimes occurs for the object (*kamma*) of a root ending in the suffixes *ṇu* and *tu*. In *kita* derivatives, the genitive case occurs as appropriate for the object of the sense of state (*bhāva*) and for the sense of the agent (*kattu*).

368. The genitive case is sometimes seen for the agent and the object of a word ending in finite verbal terminations (*ākhyāta*) such as *ti*. However, the genitive case is not seen in the sense of relation (*sambandha*) because there is no connection between a finite verb and a genitive case.

369. There are forms such as: "the maker of the deed," "the maker of the deed," "the extractor of beings," "the extractor of (of) beings." There is also: "the cook's cooking of rice" or "the cook cooks the rice."

370. "He makes the pupil recite the Dhamma," "He will not remember the kingdom." In the *Moggalāna* treatises, it is stated that the genitive case occurs in the sense of relation when the meanings of agent and others are not specifically desired.
75:
371. The suffixes *māna* and *anta* occur in the present and future times. Some teachers, however, say that the suffix *anta* occurs in all three times without exception. The suffix *anta* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattu*), while the suffix *māna* occurs in all three senses: state (*bhāva*), object (*kamma*), and agent (*kattu*).

372. "I, standing, will do, making it clear." "You will hear the word being spoken by me, which is to be established."

373. The three suffixes *tāye*, *tuṃ*, and others occur in the sense of the future state (*bhāva*) which is the result of that causal action. The elision of the dative case (*catutthī*) after words ending in those suffixes is stated in the *Moggalāna* treatise.

374. In the *Kaccāyana* and *Nyāsa* treatises, however, it is held that the two suffixes *tave* and *tuṃ* occur in the sense of the agent in all times because they are designated as *kita*.

375. In saying "He goes to do," "He desires to do," there are the forms *kattāye*, *kātuṃ*, and *kātave*. Thus, the dative sense (*sampadāna*) and the agentive sense (*kattu*) should be understood as appropriate.
76: 376. It should be known that suffixes such as tuna are generally used for verbs occurring in the preceding time among verbs having the same agent. This is because verbs having the same agent are also observed in simultaneous time (samānakāla) and subsequent time (aparakāla). 377. Although the capacities (satti) in various actions are different, they are recognized as verbs having the same agent because those agent-capacities reside in a single substance (dabba) within a single sentence. 378. In treatises such as the Kalāpa, suffixes such as tuna and tvā are prescribed in the sense of state (bhāva). In treatises such as the Kaccāyana, however, they are prescribed in the sense of the agent (kattu) because they are designated as kit. 379. Because of being designated as kit and due to the principle expressed as 'ekakattūnaṃ', in the Rūpasiddhi treatise, suffixes such as tuna are stated only in the sense of the agent. 380. Words ending in suffixes such as tvā have the meaning of an adverb (kriyā-visesana) because they qualify the main verb. Some teachers, however, state that they have the meaning of an adjective to the agent (kattu-visesana) since they occur in the sense of the agent.
77:
381. The hero (or the cook) eats after cooking. The sun rises after dispelling the darkness. Strength arises from drinking ghee. He departs, being about to close the door.

382. Rice is cooked and eaten, or it has been eaten. Although those verbs (bhujjate, bhutto) express only one object, the suffix -tvā does not express (the object).

383. Even though the suffix -tvā does not express (the object), the grammatical operation (such as the word 'odano') is accomplished solely through its connection with the principal verb. This is because, among the preceding and succeeding verbs, the subsequent principal verb is the primary one.

384. Sometimes, however, the grammatical operation (such as the accusative case ending) is accomplished solely through its connection with the subordinate verb which is a secondary quality. The sentence "Having gone to Sāvatthī for alms, he wanders" is an illustration.

385. When there are various verbs, although there should be a distinction in the grammatical operations (kāriya), it should be understood accordingly through the meaning, such as the state of having the accusative case ending and so forth.
78:
386. Just as a son killed in the darkness of night under the perception of being a dog does not come back to life even if one regards him as a son, so too, the grammatical operation established as 'Sāvatthiṃ' because of the subordinate verb 'gantvā' does not perish because of the principal verb 'carati'.

387. The intended meaning is of two kinds: general meaning (sāmañña) and specific meaning (visesa). The intention "Having cooked rice, it is given" is a general meaning. The intention "Having cooked rice, it is eaten" is a specific meaning.

388. This specific meaning of "having cooked" cannot be known in a single word like 'kāreti' and so forth; it is known only in various distinct words.

389. The suffixes -tvā, -anta, and so forth, have the meanings of state-characteristic (bhāvalakkhaṇa) and cause (hetu) as appropriate. The examples "Being Sakka, the birth occurs" and "While reciting (or because of reciting), he dwells" are their illustrations.

390. Based on the abstract meaning (bhāva) of the two words 'hutvāna' and 'nibbatti', the nominative case in 'Sakko' occurs in the sense of the genitive. Alternatively, sometimes the word 'Sakko' ending in the nominative, which is established in consideration of the subordinate word 'hutvāna', does not perish even when the principal word is considered.

391. In a sentence such as "A union arises," a union that has already arisen in the past cannot be currently arising. A union that is currently arising cannot stand as the agent (kattā) of that verb of arising. (If this is the case, the question is raised: how can the state of verb and agent be possible?)
79:
391. In the sentence "Saṃyogo jāyate" (A union arises), a union that has already occurred in the past cannot be currently arising. A union that is currently arising cannot stand as the agent of that verb of arising, "jāyate".

392. Although two objects are facing each other, because the union is not yet evident, that state is called the potential form (sattirūpa). When those two objects unite, because the union becomes evident, it is called the manifest form (vyattirūpa).

393. Since linguistic usage is accomplished according to worldly convention (loka-saṅketa), there is no use for both potentiality and manifestation. Therefore, even a meaning that is not yet manifest is spoken of figuratively as if it were manifest.

394. Sound (speech) has as its domain the meaning that is to be expressed. That sound can express both a manifest meaning and a non-manifest meaning. Indeed, only the conventional meaning is the meaning of the sound. Through that conventional meaning, the intended sense is further indicated.

395. Meanings such as "sky-flower" and so forth are non-manifest meanings. Meanings such as "man" and so forth are manifest meanings. Other wise ones say that only ultimate meanings (paramattha) such as contact (phassa) and so forth are truly manifest meanings.
80:
396. Sound has a meaning that is accomplished by worldly convention (saṅketa); it does not possess an absolutely manifest meaning alone. In truth, only the conventional meaning (sammuti-attha) conceived by the intellect is the meaning of the sound.

397. In the country named Tambadīpa, in the city called Arimaddana, the Elder Saddhammasiri composed this work, which is an analysis of the meanings of sounds containing a hidden and profound essence.

398. The treatise Saddatthabhedacintā is finished. In terms of the extent of the text, there are three hundred and ninety-seven verses, three feet (pāda), and four syllables.

399. Whosoever is skilled in analyzing the characteristics of the meanings of sounds that have determined characteristics, that person is able to know the Three Piṭakas without difficulty.

400. By this merit obtained, may I attain the incomparable and most noble (Omniscience). Having attained that, may I be one who can liberate all beings from the bonds of existence.

## The treatise Saddatthabhedacintā is finished.
